workedExamples.title: Histogram vs. bar chart: reading frequency from a bin

steps.prompt: A display shows test scores grouped into equal-width intervals: 60–69, 70–79, 80–89, 90–99. The bars touch each other with no gaps. The variable on the horizontal axis is the test score. Is the test score a NUMBER or a CATEGORY?
steps.reveal: Test score is a NUMBER. Because the horizontal axis shows a numeric variable split into equal-width intervals (called bins), and the bars touch, this is a HISTOGRAM. A bar chart shows separate CATEGORIES (like favorite color) with gaps between the bars.

steps.prompt: What is the difference between the bars TOUCHING and having GAPS?
steps.reveal: Touching bars mean the intervals are continuous pieces of a number line — 69 flows right into 70. Gaps would mean the bars are separate categories with nothing between them. The classic trap (histogram-bar-chart-confusion) is treating each bin like its own category instead of part of one continuous numeric scale.

steps.prompt: The 80–89 bin has a bar that reaches a height of 7. What does that 7 tell you?
steps.reveal: It tells you the FREQUENCY: 7 students scored somewhere in the interval 80–89. It does NOT tell you any single student's exact score. The height of a histogram bar is a count of how many data values fall inside that bin.

steps.prompt: Why can't you say '7 students scored exactly 80'?
steps.reveal: Because a bin covers a RANGE (80 through 89), not one value. Reading a bin as a single category or a single score is the histogram-bar-chart-confusion error. The bar only reports how many values landed anywhere in that whole interval.

workedExamples.title: Box plot: the five-number summary and IQR

steps.prompt: A box plot is built from a five-number summary: minimum, first quartile (Q1), median, third quartile (Q3), and maximum. This box plot has min 10, Q1 25, median 40, Q3 55, max 70. Where is the median shown on the plot?
steps.reveal: The median (40) is the line INSIDE the box, dividing the box into two parts. It is NOT the left edge of the box — that left edge is Q1 (25). Reading the median line as Q1 is a common box-plot-quartile-misread error.

steps.prompt: Which two values form the EDGES of the box?
steps.reveal: The left edge of the box is Q1 (25) and the right edge is Q3 (55). The box always spans from Q1 to Q3. The min (10) and max (70) are at the ENDS of the whiskers, not the box edges.

steps.prompt: The IQR (interquartile range) measures the spread of the middle half of the data. The formula is IQR = Q3 − Q1. Compute it.
steps.reveal: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 55 − 25 = 30. Use the two BOX EDGES, not the whisker ends. A frequent mistake is using max − min (70 − 10 = 60), which is the full range, not the IQR.

steps.prompt: Suppose someone reads the minimum (10) as if it were Q1. What IQR would they wrongly get, and why is it wrong?
steps.reveal: They would compute 55 − 10 = 45, which is wrong. Q1 is the LEFT EDGE OF THE BOX (25), not the left whisker tip (10). Mixing up the min with Q1 is the box-plot-quartile-misread trap. The correct IQR is 55 − 25 = 30.
